title: Ang 917–922: the Anand
hookLine: the song of bliss on the page
tomorrow: what did Guru Amar Das ask for, at the very end?

lines: BLISS HAS COME, O MY MOTHER.
cards: Search for how to be happy and the advice comes in two flavors: celebrate everything, or get calm. The Anand opens with both at once.
Guru Amar Das, ang 917, in paraphrase: bliss has come, O my mother, for I have found the True Guru. I found the Guru with ease, with sahaj, and in my mind the songs of celebration are playing.
Vadhaiyan: the songs sung when good news comes to a house, a birth, a wedding. So which one is bliss: the party, or the calm?

teach.b: Sikh readers hear that opening in more than one way, and both voices deserve a fair hearing.
The first voice says: bliss is rising spirits. Sikhs have a phrase for it, chardi kala, ascending spirit, a heart that stays high whatever comes. Read this way, the vadhaiyan are the point.
Something has been found, and the mind is throwing a party about it. Gloom isn't the Guru's mood. The second voice says: listen to the word before the songs.
Sahaj. Ease, poise, the natural state. Read this way, anand isn't a high held up by effort.
It's a steadiness that's there once the Guru is found, and it can sit right beside a hard day.
Later in the Anand, the text says, in paraphrase: everyone talks of bliss; bliss is known through the Guru.
Both readers lean on that line. The first hears: so be joyful, it's been given. The second hears: so stop chasing the feeling; it comes through the Guru, not by forcing it.
And the hymn itself? It puts both words in one line, sahaj and vadhaiyan, and doesn't choose. The Anand closes gurdwara programs and is sung at weddings.
A song that has to fit all of that can't be only a party, and can't be only a hush.
Bliss, in the Anand, holds both.

how: Guru Amar Das's Anand is recited by Sikhs in daily prayer; a short portion of it is sung to close gurdwara programs, and it is sung at the Anand Karaj, the Sikh wedding.

o: a page of wedding rounds sung at a Sikh wedding
where Guru Amar Das's Anand, the song of bliss, begins

games.q: inside the Anand — tap the pairs.
p: songs sung when good news comes

s: the Anand's first lines hold both sahaj and celebration songs
found with ease, and the vadhaiyan play in the mind: both in one line.
bliss, in the Anand, is a happy feeling you work yourself up to
the text says bliss is known through the Guru; both readings agree it isn't forced.
the Anand is only sung on happy occasions
it closes gurdwara programs and is sung at weddings; it has to fit more than one mood.

games.q: a friend says the Anand means 'stay cheerful, always.' you lean toward 'calm ease.' what's the best case for her side?
o: the text has celebration songs playing in the mind; the joy is real, not just calm.
she's right that bliss means never feeling sad about anything at all.
there isn't one; the Anand only ever talks about quiet and calm.
games.why: the vadhaiyan are right there in the first pauri, next to sahaj. her reading has the text on its side, and so does yours.

practice: Sit the way sahaj sounds: back easy and upright, hands open on your knees, jaw loose. Keep that ease for the sit, and if something happy comes to mind, let it play like music from another room.
If you'd like, read the first lines of ang 917 before you begin.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: anand, bliss; the Anand opens 'anand bhaiaa meree maae', bliss has come, O my mother (ang 917).

carryVoice: Bliss: in the Anand it's the songs and the ease together, and the hymn won't pick one. Sung through.
